name: Lotus shoes

lead: Lotus shoes were handmade silk slippers, often richly embroidered, worn over feet that had been bound from childhood. The ideal 'golden lotus' foot was about three Chinese inches (roughly 10-11 cm), and the small, decorated shoe was a central part of how that ideal was displayed.

Their appearance payoff was social: a small, embroidered foot signalled beauty, femininity, status and sewing skill, helping marriage prospects. Today they are studied and collected as textile and cultural artefacts.

paras: Shoes were handmade by the girls and women themselves, which also displayed their embroidery skill. They covered and supported feet already altered by binding; some women could not walk without them. Larger sizes were nicknamed silver and iron lotuses.

The binding the shoes accompanied caused chronic infection, ingrown toenails, gangrene and lasting mobility loss, and perhaps up to 10% of girls died of related infection. Foot binding has been abolished, and this entry documents history only.

angle.text: The shoes were the visible half of a historical beauty standard: a decorated three-inch shoe signalled a prized foot and the maker's skill. They are documented here as history, not as something to emulate.

lead: Lotus shoes were the small, handmade shoes made for 'lotus feet', the bound feet produced by the Chinese custom of foot binding [1]. They were often silk and elaborately embroidered.

In the beauty ideals of the time, a tiny foot was a marker of beauty, status and femininity and an aid in securing a good marriage, and the shoe was how that foot was shown while the foot itself was usually kept covered [1]. Women often made their own shoes, so embroidery doubled as a display of skill and family pride [1].
This wiki documents lotus shoes as a historical beauty object. The practice behind them left lasting harm to the women who underwent it and has been abolished.

paras: Lotus shoes were made in small sizes to fit bound feet and were generally handmade, often from silk, with decorated uppers [1]. The ideal 'golden lotus' was about three Chinese inches, with 'silver' lotuses around four and 'iron' lotuses around five or more, the last being the least desirable for marriage [1].

The shoes and wrappings were embroidered, reflecting family pride, and made shoes showed the wearer's needlework skill [1]. Some women with bound feet could not walk without their shoes, which gave support [1].

The earliest archaeological evidence of foot binding comes from Song-dynasty tombs, including those of Huang Sheng (d. 1243) and Madame Zhou (d. 1274), where Zhou's skeleton was found with narrow pointed slippers fitting her bound feet [1]. The three-inch ideal is believed to date to the Ming period [1]. Manchu 'flower bowl' platform shoes, with a raised wooden sole, imitated the swaying gait of bound feet [1]. The Zhiqian Shoe Factory in Harbin, the last to make lotus shoes, closed in 1999 [1].
No studies found on the shoes themselves. Research on foot binding includes a 1997 study of consequences among older women in Beijing [1].

The shoes accompanied foot binding, which is associated with chronic infection, ingrown toenails, gangrene, disability and lifelong mobility limits. As many as 10% of girls are thought to have died from infections caused by binding [1].
